rationale: The four CSF cohorts (Berlin, Sweden, Magdeburg, Kiel) were collected and measured separately. Shifts in protein abundance between cohorts probably add noise that is unrelated to AD and makes the L2 logistic model less reliable. I am subtracting each protein's median within its site, in a label-free step inside `featurize`, so the model compares people against others from the same cohort. If AD prevalence differs a lot between sites, this centring could also remove some real AD signal, so it needs to be checked against the current score.

The current model only sees proteins and ignores age, which is the strongest risk factor for a clinical AD diagnosis. If I just added age as one of ~800 L2-penalised columns, it would get almost no weight. Instead I stack: a grouped inner-CV out-of-fold protein-model score is combined with age and sex in a small, lightly regularised second-stage logistic model, so age gets the weight it deserves.

Low n means the full-proteome L2 model spreads its weight thinly over ~800 proteins. I'm adding a second L2 logistic model trained only on known CSF AD markers, then averaging the two models' probabilities. The markers are Bader 2020's tau-linked glycolysis and 14-3-3 proteins (SMOC1, YWHAG, SPP1, CHI3L1, MDH1, PKM, ALDOA), plus synaptic, glial and complement proteins. This prior-biology view should give a more stable signal that is less prone to overfitting. Its quantification filter is looser, because brain-derived markers are low-abundance and often missing.

I'm adding a third ensemble member: a fixed, prior-defined log-ratio score that subtracts a synaptic module from the tau/glycolysis/14-3-3 "up" module. The up module is SMOC1, YWHAG, SPP1, CHI3L1, MDH1, PKM, ALDOA and related proteins; the synaptic module is NPTX2, NPTXR, VGF and similar proteins, which fall in AD. Its only learned parts are a sign check and a 1-D Platt calibration, so it should add an almost zero-variance biological signal that small-n L2 models cannot estimate reliably on their own. Each protein is z-scored on train and averaged over the proteins that were quantified, without imputation. This also avoids the missingness bias of half-min filling for low-abundance brain proteins.

The synaptic "down" module now uses only 5 genes, and probably just 2–3 of them pass the quantification filter, so the denominator of the log-ratio is noisy. I'm adding the rest of the neuronal-pentraxin/secretogranin cluster that falls in AD CSF (NPTX1, SCG3, SCG5, CHGA, PCSK1N, CBLN4; reported by Higginbotham 2020 and Johnson 2023). Averaging more co-regulated proteins should make this prior-defined signal less noisy without adding any learned parameters.

Right now each sample is centred on the median of all its quantified proteins. Missingness depends on abundance, so samples with fewer detected low-abundance proteins get an inflated median, which mixes detection depth into the normalization. I'm changing featurize to centre each sample on the median of a fixed reference set of proteins quantified in nearly every sample. This label-free step should give a cleaner correction for CSF loading and dilution. The ensemble is unchanged.

CSF samples often carry a small, variable amount of blood, which Bader et al. 2020 flagged as a major confounder in CSF proteomics. Red blood cells are rich in the same glycolytic enzymes (GAPDH/PKM/ALDOA/ENO1/LDHB/PGK1/TPI1) and 14-3-3 proteins that our AD panel and up-module rely on. So I add a label-free step in `featurize` that builds a per-sample red-cell contamination score from haemoglobins, CA1/CA2, PRDX2, CAT and related proteins, then removes each protein's linear dependence on that score. The ensemble is unchanged.

Every sample is normalized to a reference set of near-completely quantified proteins, and that set is mostly plasma-derived (albumin, transferrin, apolipoproteins, immunoglobulins). So brain-derived AD markers end up partly measured relative to how much plasma protein has leaked across the blood–CSF barrier. That leakage varies a lot with age and with non-AD neurological disease. I reuse the label-free regress-out step that worked for blood contamination: build a per-sample plasma-leakage score from classical plasma proteins and remove each other protein's linear dependence on it.

Right now the ensemble averages probabilities. The 800-feature full-proteome logistic regression produces much more extreme probabilities than the 1-D Platt-calibrated module score, so the proteome model quietly dominates. The prior-biology members, which carry the most stable signal at small n, get little say. I'm putting the three members on a common scale instead: each one's log-odds is divided by the spread of its training-set log-odds, then the scaled log-odds are averaged. This should also down-weight members that overfit, because their in-sample spread is inflated.

I'm adding a fourth ensemble member: a diagonal LDA / shrunken-centroid-style classifier (Dudoit 2002; Tibshirani's PAM). It keeps the top 100 proteins by moderated t-statistic and weights each one independently, ignoring correlations between proteins, which is a much lower-variance inductive bias than the correlation-aware L2 logistic models at n≈110. Its score is Platt-calibrated on grouped inner-CV out-of-fold scores, not in-sample ones, so overfitting can't inflate its probabilities and let it dominate the average.

In round 1, centring each protein within its site without using labels lowered the score. The likely cause is that AD prevalence differs between cohorts, so that centring also removed real disease signal. In this version, each site's shift is estimated only from the training non-AD controls at that site, measured against the pooled training controls. The shift is shrunk towards zero when a site has few controls, then applied to train and test samples from that site. This removes the cohort measurement offset while keeping between-site differences in AD prevalence.

CSF proteomics at n≈110 contains outlier values for individual proteins, such as failed quantifications or residual contamination spikes. After standardization those values can reach |z| > 5, and they pull the L2 logistic models' weights toward a few samples. Clipping the train-standardized features at ±3 in both logistic members (winsorization) should make the learned weights more robust without discarding any proteins.

Right now each sample is centred on the median of its raw log2 intensities over the reference proteins. Because those proteins span orders of magnitude, that median effectively follows the one or two proteins nearest the middle of the abundance range, and their own biological variation leaks into every protein. I'm switching to a label-free median-of-ratios factor (DESeq / PQN style): take each reference protein's deviation from its cross-sample median, then use the per-sample median of those deviations. This weights all ~100+ reference proteins equally and should give a more stable correction for CSF loading and dilution. I haven't run it, so I don't have a score for it yet.

For low-abundance brain proteins in CSF (SMOC1, SPP1, NPTX2, VGF and similar), a missing value usually means the protein was too low to detect, not that it was missing at random. The module score currently skips missing proteins, which treats a non-detected up-module protein as if it were at the average level. I now fill non-detected module proteins with their training-set minimum (detection-limit imputation) before z-scoring, so non-detection counts as low abundance in the up-minus-down log-ratio.

The prior up/down log-ratio module averages only a handful of quantified seed proteins, so its per-sample estimate is noisy. Bader 2020 described a whole cluster of about 40 tau-correlated proteins, and the synaptic proteins also form a cluster. This change grows each module with up to 15 extra proteins from the training samples (minimum partial correlation 0.5) that move with that module's seed score. Selection uses no labels. It controls for the opposite module, so the shared CSF brain-protein / turnover axis that drives both modules is not picked up and the ratio stays focused on AD. Averaging more co-regulated proteins should reduce measurement noise in this signal without adding any label-fitted parameters. I haven't run this version, so I don't have a score for it.

The full-proteome member only uses proteins quantified in at least 70% of training samples. That cut-off drops many low-abundance brain-derived proteins (neuronal, glial and synaptic), and those are the ones most likely to differ in AD CSF. Their missing values are mostly abundance-dependent (not random), so half-minimum imputation turns non-detection into real "low abundance" information. I'm lowering the full-proteome cut-off to 50%, the same threshold the panel and module already use, and changing nothing else. I haven't run this version, so I don't have a score for it yet.

The up-module now covers only the tau/glycolysis and glial markers. It leaves out presynaptic and postsynaptic proteins that are reliably higher in AD CSF because synapses are breaking down: neurogranin (NRGN), SNAP25, GAP43, SYT1 and VAMP2. These are separate from the NPTX2/VGF neurosecretory proteins, which fall in AD. It also leaves out the rest of Bader et al.'s tau-correlated glycolysis and redox cluster (PGAM1, LDHA, ALDOC, ENO2, PPIA, PARK7, YWHAE/YWHAQ). I'm adding these established AD-increased proteins to the fixed prior up-module, so the log-ratio score averages more co-regulated disease signal and gains no new learned parameters. This is not yet run and has no score; if few of these proteins pass the 50% quantification filter, it may change little, as the round-5 down-module extension did.
